framework: AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description (effective fall 2020)
subject: Human Geography

source.licence: © College Board; structure + our own wording only

outcomes.text: Identify map types, the information maps show, and the spatial patterns and relationships they portray.
Tell reference maps from thematic maps.
Describe spatial patterns on maps: absolute and relative distance and direction, clustering, dispersal, elevation.
Explain that every map is selective and map projections distort shape, area, distance and direction.
Identify the different methods of collecting geographic data.
Recognise that data can be gathered in the field by organisations or individuals.
Name geospatial technologies: GIS, satellite navigation, remote sensing, online mapping and visualisation.
List written sources of spatial information such as field notes, media, narratives, policy documents, interviews, landscape and photo analysis.
Explain the effects of decisions made using geographic information.
Describe how census data and satellite imagery guide personal, business, organisational and government decisions at every scale.
Define major geographic concepts that show spatial relationships.
Define absolute and relative location, space, place, flows, distance decay, time-space compression and pattern.
Explain how major geographic concepts illustrate spatial relationships.
Explain nature-and-society concepts: sustainability, natural resources and land use.
Trace how ideas about people and environment moved from environmental determinism to possibilism.
Define the scales of analysis geographers use.
Name the scales: global, regional, national and local.
Explain what different scales of analysis reveal.
Show how patterns and processes at different scales give different readings of data.
Describe the different ways geographers define regions.
Explain that regions are defined by unifying characteristics or patterns of activity.
Distinguish formal, functional and perceptual (vernacular) regions.
Explain that regional boundaries are transitional, often contested and overlapping.
Apply regional analysis at local, national and global scales.

units.title: Unit 2: Population and Migration Patterns and Processes

outcomes.text: Identify the factors that influence where people live at different scales.
Explain how physical factors (climate, landforms, water) and human factors (culture, economics, history, politics) shape population distribution.
Recognise that the factors explaining distribution patterns change with the scale of analysis.
Define the methods geographers use to calculate population density.
Name and distinguish arithmetic, physiological and agricultural density.
Explain how density methods differ and what each shows.
Explain that each density method reveals a different level of pressure on the land.
Explain how population distribution and density affect society and the environment.
Explain how distribution and density affect politics, economies, social life and service provision such as health care.
Explain how distribution and density affect the environment and resources, as in carrying capacity.
Describe the elements of population composition geographers use.
Describe how age structure and sex ratio vary across regions and scales.
Explain how geographers depict and analyse population composition.
Use population pyramids to assess growth and decline and to predict markets for goods and services.
Explain factors behind historical and current population growth and decline.
Name fertility, mortality and migration as the demographic factors of growth and decline.
Use rate of natural increase and population-doubling time to explain growth and decline.
Explain how social, cultural, political and economic factors influence fertility, mortality and migration rates.
Explain theories of population growth and decline.
Use the demographic transition model to explain population change over time.
Explain how the epidemiological transition accounts for changing death rates.
Use Malthusian theory and its critiques to analyse population change and its consequences.
Explain the intent and effects of population and immigration policies.
Distinguish pronatalist, antinatalist and immigration policies that promote or discourage growth.
Explain the demographic consequences of the changing role of women in different parts of the world.
Explain how changing values and access to education, jobs, health care and contraception reduced fertility in most regions.
Explain how changing roles for women affect fertility, mortality and migration, as in Ravenstein's laws of migration.
Explain the causes and consequences of an aging population.
Explain that population aging depends on birth rates, death rates and life expectancy.
Explain the political, social and economic consequences of aging, including the dependency ratio.
Explain how different factors encourage migration.
Divide migration causes into push factors and pull factors.
Recognise that push/pull factors and intervening opportunities or obstacles may be cultural, demographic, economic, environmental or political.
Describe types of forced and voluntary migration.
Describe forced migrations: slavery and events producing refugees, internally displaced persons and asylum seekers.
Describe voluntary migrations: transnational, transhumance, internal, chain, step, guest worker and rural-to-urban.
Explain historical and current geographic effects of migration.
Explain the political, economic and cultural effects of migration.
Define the characteristics and traits geographers consider when they study culture.
Define culture as the shared practices, technologies, attitudes and behaviours a society passes on.
Give examples of culture traits such as food preferences, architecture and land use.
Contrast cultural relativism and ethnocentrism as attitudes to cultural difference.
Describe the characteristics of cultural landscapes.
Describe cultural landscapes as mixes of physical features, farming and industry, religion and language, sequent occupance and architecture and land-use patterns.
Explain how landscapes and land and resource use reflect cultural beliefs and identities.
Explain how attitudes to ethnicity and gender, ethnic neighbourhoods and indigenous lands shape the use of space.
Explain patterns and landscapes of language, religion, ethnicity and gender.
Explain how regional patterns of language, religion and ethnicity build sense of place, placemaking and the global cultural landscape.
Explain how language, ethnicity and religion create centripetal and centrifugal forces.
Define the types of diffusion.
Distinguish relocation diffusion from expansion diffusion (contagious, hierarchical, stimulus).
Explain how historical processes shape present cultural patterns.
Explain how culture traits meeting global forces create new cultural forms, as in creolization and lingua franca.
Explain how colonialism, imperialism and trade shaped cultural patterns and practices.
Explain how cultural ideas are socially constructed and changed by urbanization, globalization, media, technology, politics and economics.
Explain how the internet and time-space convergence reshape culture, spreading English, eroding indigenous languages, and causing convergence and divergence.
Explain what leads to the diffusion of universalizing and ethnic religions.
Explain that language families, languages, dialects, religions, ethnic cultures and gender roles diffuse from cultural hearths.
Read the diffusion of language families such as Indo-European and of religions on maps, charts and toponyms.
Explain that religions have places of origin and spread by different processes shaped by their practices and beliefs.
Explain that universalizing religions (Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, Sikhism) spread by expansion and relocation diffusion.
Explain that ethnic religions (Hinduism, Judaism) stay near their hearth or spread by relocation diffusion.
Explain how diffusion changes the cultural landscape.
Define acculturation, assimilation, syncretism and multiculturalism as effects of cultural diffusion.
Define the types of political entities on world political maps.
Explain that independent states are the main building blocks of the world political map.
Distinguish nations, nation-states, stateless nations, multinational states, multistate nations and autonomous or semiautonomous regions.
Explain the processes that shaped modern political geography.
Explain how sovereignty, nation-states and self-determination shape the contemporary world.
Explain how colonialism, imperialism, independence movements and devolution shaped political boundaries.
Describe political power and territoriality as geographers use them.
Explain political power as control over people, land and resources, as in neocolonialism, shatterbelts and choke points.
Define territoriality as the link between people, their culture and economy, and the land.
Define the types of political boundaries geographers use.
Distinguish relict, superimposed, subsequent, antecedent, geometric and consequent boundaries.
Explain the nature and function of international and internal boundaries.
Explain that boundaries are defined, delimited, demarcated and administered to limit sovereignty but are often contested.
Explain that boundaries often follow cultural, national or economic divisions, but some come from DMZs or policy such as the Berlin Conference.
Explain how land and maritime boundaries and agreements influence identity, interaction and resource disputes.
Explain how the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea sets rights over international waters, territorial seas and exclusive economic zones.
Explain how voting districts, redistricting and gerrymandering affect election results at various scales.
Define federal and unitary states.
Distinguish unitary states from federal states as forms of governance.
Explain how federal and unitary states affect spatial organization.
Contrast top-down centralised unitary governance with locally based, dispersed power in federal states.
Define the factors that lead to the devolution of states.
Name devolution factors: physical division of groups, ethnic separatism, ethnic cleansing, terrorism, economic and social problems and irredentism.
Explain how political, economic, cultural and technological change challenges state sovereignty.
Explain devolution as states fragmenting into autonomous regions or units, or disintegrating as in Sudan and the former Soviet Union.
Explain how communication technology has helped devolution, supranationalism and democratization.
Explain how transnational challenges, economies of scale, trade agreements and military alliances promote supranationalism.
Explain how supranational bodies (UN, NATO, EU, ASEAN, Arctic Council, African Union) can limit member states' actions and challenge sovereignty.

topics.title: 4.10 Consequences of Centrifugal and Centripetal Forces

subtopics.title: Consequences of Centrifugal and Centripetal Forces

outcomes.text: Explain how centrifugal and centripetal forces apply at the state scale.
Explain how centrifugal forces can lead to failed states, uneven development, stateless nations and ethnic nationalist movements.
Explain how centripetal forces can lead to ethnonationalism, fairer infrastructure and greater cultural cohesion.

units.title: Unit 5: Agriculture and Rural Land-Use Patterns and Processes

outcomes.text: Explain the link between physical geography and agricultural practices.
Explain how the physical environment and climates, such as Mediterranean and tropical, influence farming.
Name intensive farming practices: market gardening, plantation agriculture and mixed crop-livestock systems.
Name extensive farming practices: shifting cultivation, nomadic herding and ranching.
Identify rural settlement patterns and the methods used to survey rural land.
Explain that specific farming practices shape different rural land-use patterns.
Classify rural settlement patterns as clustered, dispersed or linear.
Name rural survey methods: metes and bounds, township and range, and long lot.
Identify the major centres where plants and animals were domesticated.
Locate early domestication hearths: Fertile Crescent, Indus Valley, Southeast Asia and Central America.
Explain how plants and animals spread around the world.
Explain how diffusion, such as the Columbian Exchange and agricultural revolutions, spread plants and animals globally.
Explain the advances and impacts of the second agricultural revolution.
Explain how new technology and more food led to better diets, longer lives and more factory workers.
Explain the Green Revolution's consequences for food supply and the environment in developing regions.
Describe the Green Revolution: high-yield seeds, more chemicals and mechanised farming.
Weigh the positive and negative consequences of the Green Revolution for people and the environment.
Explain how economic forces influence agricultural practices.
Explain that production regions are defined by subsistence or commercial practice, such as monocropping.
Use bid-rent theory to explain how land costs determine intensive versus extensive farming.
Explain how large commercial operations are replacing small family farms.
Explain how complex commodity chains link production and consumption of farm products.
Explain how technology raised economies of scale and the land's carrying capacity.
Describe how the von Thunen model explains agricultural production patterns at various scales.
Explain how von Thunen links land use to transport costs from market, and why specialty regions may not fit his rings.
Explain the interdependence among regions of agricultural production and consumption.
Explain that food and farm products travel through a global supply chain.
Explain how some countries depend heavily on one or more export commodities.
Explain how politics, infrastructure and world trade patterns shape global food distribution.
Explain the environmental and societal consequences of agricultural practices.
List environmental effects: pollution, land cover change, desertification, soil salinization and conservation efforts.
Explain how slash and burn, terraces, irrigation, deforestation, draining wetlands, shifting cultivation and pastoral nomadism alter landscapes.
Describe societal effects: changing diets, women's roles in production and economic purpose.
Explain challenges and debates around contemporary agriculture and food production.
Explain debates over biotechnology, GMOs and aquaculture: sustainability, soil and water use, biodiversity and chemical use.
Explain how food-choice movements (urban farming, CSA, organic, fair trade, local food, dietary shifts) shape production and consumption.
Explain challenges of feeding the world: food insecurity, food deserts, distribution problems, weather and land lost to suburbs.
Explain how processing and market locations, economies of scale, distribution and policy affect food production.
Explain geographic variations in women's roles in food production and consumption.
Explain how women's roles in producing, distributing and consuming food vary with the type of production.

units.title: Unit 6: Cities and Urban Land-Use Patterns and Processes

topics.title: 6.1 The Origin and Influences of Urbanization

subtopics.title: The Origin and Influences of Urbanization

outcomes.text: Explain the processes that start and drive urbanization and suburbanization.
Explain how site and situation influence a city's origin, function and growth.
Explain how transport and communication, population growth, migration, economic development and policy drive urbanization.
Describe megacities and metacities as outcomes of urbanization, increasingly in periphery and semiperiphery countries.
Describe how suburbanization, sprawl and decentralisation created edge cities, exurbs and boomburbs and new challenges.
Explain how cities embody globalization.
Explain that world cities sit atop the urban hierarchy and drive globalization.
Explain that cities are linked by global networks and mediate global processes.

topics.title: 6.4 The Size and Distribution of Cities

subtopics.title: The Size and Distribution of Cities

outcomes.text: Identify urban concepts such as hierarchy, interdependence, relative size and spacing that explain city distribution and interaction.
Apply the rank-size rule, primate city, gravity and Christaller's central place theory to city size and distribution.
Explain the internal structure of cities using models and theories.
Use the Burgess, Hoyt, Harris-Ullman, galactic city and bid-rent models and Latin American, Southeast Asian and African city models.
Explain how low-, medium- and high-density housing show different patterns of residential land use.
Explain how residential buildings and land use reflect and shape a city's culture, technology, development cycles and infilling.
Explain how a city's infrastructure relates to local politics, society and the environment.
Explain how infrastructure location and quality affect patterns of economic and social development.
Identify urban design initiatives and zoning practices.
Name sustainable design ideas: mixed land use, walkability, transit-oriented development, smart growth, New Urbanism, greenbelts and slow-growth cities.
Explain the effects of different urban design initiatives.
Weigh praise (less sprawl, walkability, housing variety, livability) against criticism (costs, de facto segregation, lost character).
Explain how qualitative and quantitative data show the causes and effects of change in cities.
Use census and survey data to show changes in urban population size and composition.
Use field studies and narratives to show individual attitudes to urban change.
Explain the causes and effects of geographic change within urban areas.
Explain urban challenges: housing issues such as redlining, blockbusting and affordability; services; crime; environmental injustice; disamenity zones.
Explain the growth of squatter settlements and land-tenure conflicts in large cities.
Name responses such as inclusionary zoning and local food movements.
Weigh the positive and negative consequences of urban renewal and gentrification.
Explain how fragmented government across state, county, city and neighbourhood levels complicates urban problems.
Describe how effective different attempts to address urban sustainability are.
List challenges: sprawl, sanitation, climate change, air and water quality, ecological footprint and energy use.
List responses: regional planning, brownfield redevelopment, urban growth boundaries and farmland protection.

units.title: Unit 7: Industrial and Economic Development Patterns and Processes

outcomes.text: Explain how the Industrial Revolution drove the growth and spread of industrialization.
Explain that industrialization began with new technologies and was helped by natural resources.
Explain how industrialization raised food supplies and populations, moved workers to city jobs and changed class structures.
Explain how industrial investors' hunt for raw materials and markets fed colonialism and imperialism.
Explain the spatial patterns of industrial production and development.
Distinguish primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary sectors and their development patterns.
Explain how labour, transport, break-of-bulk points, least cost theory, markets and resources shape manufacturing location in core, semiperiphery and periphery.
Describe social and economic measures of development.
List measures: GDP, GNP, GNI per capita, economy structure, income distribution, fertility, infant mortality, health care, energy use and literacy.
Describe measures of gender inequality such as the Gender Inequality Index.
Use the Human Development Index to show differences in development among states.
Explain how economic development has changed gender parity.
Explain that women's roles change as countries develop.
Explain that more women work but still lack equal pay and opportunities.
Explain how microloans help women start local businesses and raise living standards.
Explain different theories of economic and social development.
Use Rostow's stages, Wallerstein's world system, dependency theory and commodity dependence to explain uneven development.
Explain causes and consequences of recent economic change, such as trade growth, deindustrialisation and interdependence.
Explain complementarity and comparative advantage as the basis of trade.
Explain how neoliberal policies and free trade created bodies like the EU, WTO, Mercosur and OPEC that deepen globalisation.
Explain how government initiatives such as tariffs affect development.
Explain how debt crises, lenders like the IMF and strategies like microlending connect economies.

topics.title: 7.7 Changes as a Result of the World Economy

subtopics.title: Changes as a Result of the World Economy

outcomes.text: Explain how outsourcing and restructuring cut core-region jobs and raised jobs in newly industrialised countries.
Explain special economic zones, free-trade zones, export-processing zones and the international division of labour.
Explain post-Fordist production, multiplier effects, economies of scale, agglomeration, just-in-time delivery, service and high-tech sectors and growth poles.
Explain how sustainability principles relate to industrialisation and spatial development.
Explain how sustainable development policy tackles resource depletion, mass consumption, pollution and climate change.
Explain ecotourism as nature-based tourism that can protect threatened places while providing local jobs.
Explain how the UN Sustainable Development Goals measure progress, such as small-scale finance and public transport.
